figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Illustration of Reference Sliding Window Attention (R-SWA). Each generated token attends to all reference tokens (visual tokens in OCR) and the preceding $n$ output tokens (128 by default). Compared to standard full attention, R-SWA maintains a constant KV cache throughout decoding. Compared to vanilla SWA, it preserves visual token fidelity by excluding them from state transitions, thereby avoiding progressive blurring.
figures.headline: R-SWA attends to all reference tokens and a fixed window of preceding outputs, keeping the KV cache constant during decoding.
citing_sentences: We introduce Reference Sliding Window Attention (R-SWA), illustrated in Figure 1.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Inspired by the process of humans copying books, we propose the Unlimited OCR. This model features a unified end-to-end architecture, consisting of an encoder and a MoE-LLM decoder in which all attention mechanisms are R-SWA. The KV cache is implemented as a queue with a capacity of $m+n$—each time a new token is generated, the KV corresponding to the $(m+1)$-th token in the queue is evicted, ensuring that both computational cost and memory usage do not progressively increase during the generation process.
figures.headline: The KV cache is a fixed-size queue that evicts the oldest entry on each new token, so memory stays bounded during generation.
citing_sentences: As illustrated in Figure 2, when a person copies a book by hand, their attention typically centers on three points: the original source book, a small portion of what has just been written (usually only a few characters), and the next character about to be written.
As shown in Figure 2, Unlimited OCR adopts DeepSeek OCR as its baseline.
In essence, R-SWA constrains attention within a two-segment window of size $m+n$, as illustrated in Figure 2.

abstract: Recently, end-to-end OCR models, exemplified by DeepSeek OCR, have once again thrust OCR into the spotlight. A widely held view is that employing a large language model (LLM) as the decoder allows the model to leverage the prior distribution of language, leading to improved OCR performance. However, the downside is equally evident: as the output sequence lengthens, the accumulated KV cache drives up memory consumption and progressively slows down generation. This stands in stark contrast to humans, who exhibit no such decline in efficiency during long-horizon copying tasks. In this technical report, we propose Unlimited OCR, a model designed to emulate human parsing working memory. Taking DeepSeek OCR as the baseline, we replace all attention layers in the decoder with our proposed Reference Sliding Window Attention (R-SWA), which reduces attention computation costs while maintaining a constant KV cache throughout the entire decoding process. By combining the high compression rate of DeepSeek OCR’s encoder with our constant KV cache design, Unlimited OCR can transcribe dozens of pages of documents in a single forward pass under a standard maximum length of 32K. More importantly, R-SWA is a general-purpose parsing attention mechanism — beyond OCR, it is equally applicable to tasks such as ASR, translation, etc. Codes and model weights are publicly available at http://github.com/baidu/Unlimited-OCR.

sections.body: The introduction argues that existing OCR models, including DeepSeek OCR, process documents page by page and reset memory at each step. The authors state that this is an engineering workaround rather than a general solution. They propose Reference Sliding Window Attention (R-SWA), in which each output token attends to all visual and prompt tokens and only to the preceding n output tokens, with n defaulting to 128. The stated aim is a constant KV cache during inference, lower memory use, and lower computational cost. The section lists the contributions: R-SWA, the Unlimited OCR model built on it, and a preliminary check on OCR tasks.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Current OCR models cannot parse ten pages in one pass, so the paper proposes constant-memory attention for long-horizon parsing.

sections.body: The related-work section groups prior work into pipeline OCR, end-to-end dense OCR models, high-compression encoders, and high-efficiency decoders. It notes that current end-to-end OCR models are typically under 3B parameters, and that DeepSeek OCR uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with 500M activated parameters during inference. It states that in current models the KV cache grows continuously with the decoding context, which limits both generation speed and length. The authors identify this as the issue Unlimited OCR is designed to address. The section does not report new experimental results.
sections.heading: Related Works
sections.headline: Prior end-to-end OCR decoders grow their KV cache with output length, which limits speed and length, so the paper builds on DeepSeek OCR.

sections.body: The method section defines R-SWA with a prefix segment of length `L_m` that all later tokens attend to, and a causal window of width n over generated tokens. The cache formula gives `L_m` plus min(n, T) after T generated tokens, bounded by `L_m` plus n, where standard attention gives `L_m` plus T. The authors state that the prefix stays fixed within a pass and that visual tokens are encoded once and are not updated by state transitions. The DeepEncoder is kept from DeepSeek OCR, with a 1024x1024 Base mode and a Gundam mode. The section gives no accuracy numbers, which appear in later sections.
sections.heading: Methodology
sections.headline: Reference Sliding Window Attention lets each token see all visual and prompt tokens plus the preceding 128 output tokens, keeping the cache constant.

sections.body: The data engine uses approximately 2 million document OCR samples with a 9:1 ratio of single-page to multi-page data. Single-page annotations come from Paddle OCR, and about 200k multi-page samples of 2 to 50 pages are built by concatenation with a page separator. Training continues from the DeepSeek OCR checkpoint for 4,000 steps with a global batch size of 256 and a maximum sequence length of 32K on 8x16 A800 GPUs. The DeepEncoder is frozen and only the LLM parameters are trained, with an initial learning rate of 1e-4. The section gives no evaluation results.
sections.heading: Experimental Settings
sections.headline: Training uses about 2 million document samples, with synthetic multi-page data, and continues from the DeepSeek OCR checkpoint for 4,000 steps.

sections.body: The evaluation uses OmniDocBench v1.5 and v1.6 for document parsing, and an in-house long-horizon test set with books of 2, 5, 10, 20, and 40+ pages. Table 1 lists the overall score for Unlimited OCR at 93.23 on v1.5 against 87.01 for DeepSeek OCR, and 93.92 on v1.6. The text reports that the text edit distance drops by 0.035 and the table TEDS improves by 5.96% relative to DeepSeek OCR on v1.5. The authors describe the v1.6 result as effective and lossless for single-page document OCR. The comparison set includes many other end-to-end models of different sizes.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: Unlimited OCR scores 93.23 on OmniDocBench v1.5, above DeepSeek OCR's 87.01, and 93.92 on v1.6.

sections.body: Table 4 compares theoretical tokens per second (TPS) for DeepSeek OCR and Unlimited OCR across output lengths, with a prefill length of 10 and other settings identical. At 256 tokens the two models run at virtually the same speed. As output length grows, DeepSeek OCR's TPS steadily declines, and the text says it lags behind Unlimited OCR, which uses R-SWA, by 35% at 6,000 tokens. The authors state that consistent generation speed is a critical requirement for long-horizon OCR tasks.
sections.heading: Efficiency Analysis
sections.headline: At 6,000 tokens, DeepSeek OCR's generation speed falls 35% behind Unlimited OCR, which keeps a stable rate as output grows.

sections.body: The limitations section states that the model cannot parse without limit under a finite context length such as 32K, because the prefill grows as pages accumulate. Even with DeepEncoder's high compression for image tokens, the prefill becomes very long. The short-term plan is to train with longer contexts, such as 128K, to prefill more pages. The long-term plan is a prefill pool from which the model learns to fetch KV chunks, simulating a reader flipping through pages. The authors also plan to apply R-SWA to reference-based tasks such as ASR and translation.
sections.heading: Limitation and Future Work
sections.headline: Unlimited OCR is not truly unlimited because prefill length still grows with page count, so the authors plan longer contexts.

sections.body: The conclusion restates that Unlimited OCR and R-SWA support long-horizon parsing. The authors report that when all standard attention in the decoder of an end-to-end model is replaced with causal reference-based sliding window attention, performance on parsing tasks remains lossless. They interpret this as the model learning to pass useful information from historical outputs into the window. They relate this soft forgetting to how people transcribe a book. The authors expect R-SWA to be applied to more tasks, so that attention computation and memory footprint are no longer the bottleneck for long-horizon parsing.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Replacing all decoder attention with R-SWA leaves parsing performance lossless, and the authors expect wider use beyond OCR.

sections.body: The author list gives the core contributors Youyang Yin, Huanhuan Liu, and YY, followed by a list of further contributors. The marker key states that an asterisk indicates the project leader and a dagger indicates the technical director. Huanhuan Liu is marked with an asterisk and YY with a dagger. The section contains no results or methods.
